newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia 97/98 wheat crop seen at 17.82 MT.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia 97/98 wheat crop seen at 17.82 MT.

text.p: The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) has boosted its forecast of Australia's 1997/98 (April-March) wheat crop to 17.82 million tonnes.
The increase, in ABARE's March quarter Australian Commodities bulletin, is up from the 16.98 million tonnes forecast at ABARE's Outlook conference in February.
Australia produced a record 23.50 million tonnes of wheat in 1996/97, ABARE said.
The latest estimate of 1996/97 production is up from 23.12 million tonnes forecast in February and 21.3 million tonnes forecast last December.
Australia's 24.2 percent decline in wheat production in 1997/98 would be accompanied by a 5.6 percent decline in exports by volume and a 15.4 percent decline by value, ABARE forecasts.

The volume of exports was forecast to decline to 14.5 million tonnes in 1997/98 from a forecast 15.37 million tonnes in 1996/97, while the value of exports was forecast to decline to A$2.68 billion from A$3.17 billion.
Australian prices in 1997/98 were forecast to drop by 8.8 percent, with the benchmark Australian Standard White (ASW) pool return down to A$176 a tonne from A$193 a tonne in 1996/97.
ASW pool prices fell by an estimated 25 percent in 1996/97 but record exports by the Australian Wheat Board limited the fall in returns, ABARE said.
Australian pool returns were expected to decline further in 1997/98 with falling world prices, it said.
Australian wheat plantings were forecast to contract to 10.5 million hectares in 1997/98 in response to expected lower world wheat prices and stronger prices for oilseeds and prime lambs, ABARE said.
High yields of the past two years would require increased use of inputs to achieve high yields in 1997/98, it said.
"Consequently, with yields assumed to return to average, production is expected to fall more than the decline in area," it said.

World wheat production was expected to decline in 1997/98, by 0.7 percent to 577 million tonnes, but availability was expected to increase because of the carryover of wheat from record crops in Australia, Argentina and the European Union in their 1996/97 marketing years, it said.
More wheat was expected to be held in importing countries by the end of the 1996/97 marketing year and wheat availability may be understated, ABARE said.
Note: p= preliminary; f= ABARE forecast
